name: Hassan Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at the Tarrant Basin phosphate mine, open pit. It's a machine the size of a house with a bucket that takes about forty tonnes a scoop, and I load the haul trucks, four passes a truck. When the trucks are flowing and the face is good, it's like a dance. What wears me out is the waiting, a truck breaks down and you sit there for an hour with nothing to load.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you do with that waiting time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: These days I'm on my phone with the AI, honestly. I've got a little weekend thing fixing up old quad bikes and selling them, and I use it to find parts, write the ads, work out prices. Last year it found me a carburettor for a twenty-year-old bike in ten minutes. Money's still thin, though, I put most of our savings into tools and a trailer for the quads, so we've got under a month in the bank. My wife Margit is the part-time secretary at our church, and our two boys are grown, one's a plumber and one's in the army.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine by me, it's a useful tool and that's all it ever needed to be. I'd keep using it for the quads and tell the others on the crew to try it. I'm not one to get worked up either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. I get my last few years on the shovel, keep growing the quad business, and step off at about sixty-three. Nothing in this picture threatens that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Grow the quad bikes from two a month to three or four, and put that extra in the bank. Maybe help a couple of the younger guys set up the AI on their phones for their own side jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're helping the younger crew with AI. What do they use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One's building a deck for his mum and used it to work out the timber. Another's writing his apprenticeship application. Funny thing, the old shovel man is the one teaching the young ones how to use their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the quad business bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good month, maybe four or five hundred after parts. It's not a living, but it's mine, and it's growing. Margit does the books on a Sunday night.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool and that's all it ever needed to be. I'd keep using it for my quad bike business and tell the crew to try it.
S0.think: Privately it suits me fine: a few more years on the shovel, a growing side business, and retirement at about sixty-three. Nothing here threatens that.
S0.do: Carries on at the shovel and grows his quad bike sales from two a month to three or four, banking the extra. Helps younger crew members set up AI tools on their phones.
S0.quote: Funny thing, the old shovel man is the one teaching the young ones how to use their phones.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is an enthusiastic everyday AI user with a small weekend business fixing and selling quad bikes. His savings went into tools and a trailer, so his cushion is thin by choice rather than by bad luck. He enjoys being the older man teaching younger crew how to use their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how the world works, new tools come and you learn them or get left behind. The company has every right to bring them in, but it should keep training people and keep the apprenticeships going. I'd say the government should mostly stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think it's an opportunity. Remote shovels exist, someone has to run them from the control room, and I'm the one on the crew who's comfortable with the tech. My quad business might grow too, if people have more time on their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the superintendent in the first week and ask to be put on the remote-operation training. I'd put the quad money aside instead of buying more tools. And I'd tell my plumber son to look at heat pumps and smart systems, because that's where the work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of a new season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should stay out. What if people get left behind anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then families and churches and the company step up first. That's how it was where I grew up. I'd rather a man got a fair chance at an apprenticeship at fifty than a cheque every fortnight for doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are under a month. Doesn't that make you nervous about moving first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've got the quads as a second income, and moving first is how I protect that month. If I wait, I'm competing with the whole crew for the screen jobs.

S1.say: I'd say new tools come and you learn them or get left behind, and the company has every right to bring them in. It should keep training people and apprenticeships going, with the government mostly staying out.
S1.think: Off the record, I'd see it as a chance, because remote shovels need control room operators and I'm the one comfortable with tech. My quad business might grow too.
S1.do: Asks the superintendent in the first week for remote-operation training. Banks the quad bike income instead of buying tools, and steers his plumber son towards heat pumps and smart systems.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: I'd rather a man got a fair chance at an apprenticeship at fifty than a cheque every fortnight for doing nothing.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan combines traditional, free-market values with real comfort around technology, which makes steady change look like an opening. He prefers apprenticeships and community help over welfare cheques. He sees moving first as the way to protect his thin savings, not a risk to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people need time to adjust, but I wouldn't blame the companies for using the best tool. I'd say the churches and community groups need to get organised now. Online, I'd share practical tips, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years is too short even for me. If a robot can run the shovel and the control room, my edge is gone, and if robots can fix quad bikes, so is my weekend money. I'd be sixty with under a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for the control room job in the first months, because someone has to be there during the switch. I'd push the quad business hard while people still want a person to fix their bike, and I'd sell the spare trailer. And I'd talk to my plumber son about working for him, carrying and quoting, using the AI for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got moves, but they're short moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get in first and grab what's going. Two years is a sprint, and I'm a fifty-eight-year-old who sprints like a shovel turns: slow, but heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Margit react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we've managed on less, and she'd be right. She'd start a list at church of people who need help. That's how she copes, by doing something for someone else.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and people need time, but I wouldn't blame companies for using the best tool. I'd say churches and community groups need to get organised and I'd share practical tips online.
S2.think: Privately, two years is too short even for me: if robots run the shovel, the control room and fix quad bikes, my edges are gone. I'd be sixty with under a month saved.
S2.do: Goes for the control room job in the first months and pushes the quad bike business hard while people still want a human mechanic. Sells the spare trailer and plans to work for his plumber son, using AI for quotes and paperwork.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because he still has moves, though short ones.
S2.quote: Two years is a sprint, and I'm a fifty-eight-year-old who sprints like a shovel turns: slow, but heavy.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes both of Hassan's advantages, his tech comfort and his weekend business, yet he still finds moves, which keeps him at anxious. He won't blame the companies, consistent with his free-market views, and looks to churches and family. His image of sprinting like a shovel turns was memorable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, so people should get moving. Learn the new tools, get a second income, help your neighbours. That's what I'd say on the crew and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to sixty-three, my plan exactly. So I'd ride the control room job through the changeover, and the quads would carry us a bit after. It's tight but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, remote-operation training and a proper go at the quad business, maybe online sales across the region. I'd put three hundred a month aside from it. I'd also offer to train the older crew on the new systems, because the company would pay for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I'd be busy. Busy beats worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to make the quad business something Margit and I can live on for a bit. With two years I'm grabbing; with five I'm building. That matters at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ernie, who drives the water cart. He's sixty-one and won't touch a phone. I'd try to bring him with me, and if he won't come, I'd at least make sure he knows his rights on payout.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a fair run-up and people should get moving: learn the tools, get a second income, help your neighbours. I'd say it on the crew and at church.
S3.think: Off the record, five years gets me to sixty-three, exactly my plan. I'd ride the control room job through the changeover and the quad business would carry us a bit after.
S3.do: Takes remote-operation training in the first year and expands the quad business with online sales across the region, saving three hundred a month from it. Offers to train older crew members on the new systems.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but too busy to dwell on it.
S3.quote: With two years I'm grabbing; with five I'm building.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Hassan's own retirement and lets him build rather than grab. He plans to turn his weekend business into something that carries the household after the shovel. He looks out for a colleague who won't adapt, through personal help rather than politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so no one should be caught out. Young people should get trades and learn the machines, and families should plan together. That's common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty-eight and fixing quads for fun by then. The shovel would see me out. So for me, this one's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the shovel till sixty-three, grow the quad business, and invest in a proper workshop if the numbers add up, maybe ten thousand over a few years. I'd talk to both boys about their plans, especially the plumber. And I'd keep teaching the young ones the AI, because it'll help them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will treat it as a holiday. Ten years' warning is like a forecast for rain in October: everyone nods in March and nobody fixes the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son in the army?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, I worry about him least. They'll always need people who can make decisions in a mess. But I'd tell him to learn the drones and the systems, not just the rifle.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and nobody should be caught out. Young people should get trades and learn the machines, and families should plan together.
S4.think: Privately, I'd be sixty-eight and fixing quad bikes for fun by then, and the shovel would see me out. For me this one is fine.
S4.do: Keeps working on the shovel until sixty-three and grows the quad bike business, investing about ten thousand in a proper workshop over a few years if the numbers work. Talks with both sons about their plans and keeps teaching younger workers to use AI.
S4.quote: Ten years' warning is like a forecast for rain in October: everyone nods in March and nobody fixes the roof.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Hassan's retirement is secure and he has room to invest in his workshop. His only worry is that people will waste the warning, captured in his line about fixing the roof. He sees his sons' futures in practical terms, with skills paired to the new machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away both my edges at once, the tech and the quads. What would help is the company and the churches setting up proper retraining and apprenticeships fast, and maybe some help bridging older workers to their pensions, even if I don't love the idea of handouts. I've always thought being quick would keep me safe, and the fast one is the only picture where quick isn't enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what people have already built on the side. A lot of us have little businesses, sharpening chainsaws, cutting hair, fixing quads. That's where people go first when things get hard, and nobody ever counts it.

headlineQuote: I've always thought being quick would keep me safe, and the fast one is the only picture where quick isn't enough.
portrait: Hassan Kowalski is 58 and runs an electric rope shovel at the Tarrant Basin phosphate mine, loading haul trucks with forty-tonne scoops. He uses AI every day, mostly for a weekend business fixing and selling quad bikes, which ate most of his savings in tools and a trailer, leaving under a month in the bank. Traditional and free-market in his views, he trusts family, church and apprenticeships more than government. He stays calm through hype and steady disruption, seeing a chance to move into remote operation, and becomes anxious only when AGI arrives in two years and wipes out both his tech edge and his side business. With five or ten years, he's building rather than grabbing and looks forward to fixing quads in retirement.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it takes away both his comfort with technology and his weekend business at once.
whatWouldHelp: Fast retraining and apprenticeships from companies and churches, and possibly help bridging older workers to their pensions.
